definition: Three named methods for choosing where a new in-between drawing sits between two existing keys — halves (bisect the remaining space), thirds (take a third of the remaining space), and favors (move a small, unmeasured amount toward the destination with no fixed fraction) — ordered from most frames required to fewest.
purpose: Match the METHOD used to place an in-between to how many frames are actually available and how snappy the transition should read, rather than using one subdivision method for every situation.
visible_effect: Halves produces a smooth, evenly-graduated approach; thirds produces a visibly snappier build or loss of momentum; favors produces the snappiest read of the three, since the in-between sits close to one of the two keys rather than partway between them.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Lets an animator hit a target "snappiness" deliberately rather than by accident — the video frames favors specifically as the rescue technique when there are almost no frames left to work with ("in a pinch... just favor both keyframes").
physical_interpretation: None of the three is claimed as more physically correct than another — this is a practical drawing-order convention, not a physics model.
use_cases: many available in-between frames and a desire for an even, textbook ease — halves
quickly building or shedding momentum with a moderate number of frames — thirds
very few frames available (the video's own example: four frames for a full ease-in/ease-out) — favors on both keyframes
non_use_cases: a transition that should read as perfectly uniform/mechanical, where any of these three would introduce unwanted ease
treating the three as interchangeable regardless of the actual frame budget — the video's own point is that the right method depends on how many frames are available
interactions: Slow in/slow out — these are three concrete METHODS for authoring the spacing that principle already covers at a conceptual level

Asymmetric spacing preference (W01 video 8) — a sibling entry naming the same "favor" technique as a deliberate unbalanced-distribution preference; this entry adds the two other rungs of the same ladder (halves, thirds) and the frame-budget logic for choosing between all three
DPS floor for short actions (this batch, video 11) — the fewer frames a phase has to begin with, the further down this ladder (toward favors) the choice is pushed
cadence_representation: Not directly represented. `acceleration_contrast`/`spacing_evenness` already choose an EASING CURVE on the two keys that already bound a phase (continuous, not a discrete subdivision choice), which can approximate the SHAPE these methods produce but not the underlying method of placing a specific new in-between key at a fractional time — the same "cannot add a key" limitation the `hold_length` dimension already states honestly.
control_surface: None directly; `acceleration_contrast`/`spacing_evenness` are the nearest existing levers for the resulting curve shape, not the placement method itself.
detection_and_measurement_methods: `ai/motion.js sampleMotion`'s per-frame velocity/acceleration curve could in principle distinguish a halves-shaped curve (graduated, symmetric-feeling) from a favors-shaped one (a sharp, late spike close to one key) after the fact, but nothing in this build currently classifies a measured curve into one of these three named categories.
generation_or_modification_methods: None — every strategy in `ai/plan.js` edits a rotation value or easing style at a key that already exists; none of the three methods described here can be authored by inserting a NEW key at a chosen fractional position, since no strategy in this build may add a key at all (the same limitation named under `hold_length`).
failure_modes: using halves (many in-betweens) inside a frame budget too small to support it, producing the exact "only three poses for a run cycle" problem named under `dps_floor_for_short_actions`, for a different underlying reason (too little DPS)
using favors when there is actually room for a fuller, graduated ease, leaving the transition snappier/rougher than intended
roblox_considerations: None specific — a pure 2D-drawing-authoring vocabulary; the resulting CURVE SHAPE is what would cross into Roblox's own Animation Editor easing, not the subdivision method itself.
examples: an ease-in from key A to breakdown C computed by repeated bisection, walked through with exact frame numbers (video @ 6:42–6:53)
a hammer-slam's wind-up given one "favor" in-between rather than a measured fraction, described as wanting the wind-up "a little slower" with "just one in-between" (video @ 9:44–9:52)
the video's own rescue case: an ease-in/ease-out built from only four total frames by favoring both keyframes (video @ 7:56–8:01)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/6UXjRCORV44 @ 6:59–8:01 — the three methods (halves, thirds, favors) are named and defined verbatim in the transcript; the numeric halves demonstration (@ 6:42–6:53) and the hammer-slam favor demonstration (@ 9:44–9:52) both fall inside this session's uncaptured 1:32–8:18 and 8:18–12:18 stretches (only 22 scene-change frames were selected across this 12:41 video, per the tool's own sparse-coverage warning for videos this length) — the software timeline WAS glimpsed once at t=8:18 showing a real multi-row exposure sheet, consistent with but not direct proof of the specific frame numbers spoken; experimental until validated
